label: Where automation plugs in: APIs, CI testing, ticketing and escalation

mentor.diagnosis: You treated automation as one capability rather than as a set of integration points. The exam asks which point in the workflow the automation sits at.
contrast: Integration point
What it automates
What it buys
APIs and integrations
Systems acting on each other without a human relaying
The plumbing everything else depends on
Continuous integration and testing
Security checks running on every commit and build
Flaws found while they are cheap, before release
Ticket creation
Raising a tracked work item from an alert or a finding
Nothing is lost between detection and someone owning it
Escalation
Routing onward automatically when nobody responds in time
Removes the single point of failure of one unavailable person
Enabling and disabling access
Provisioning and revoking as roles change or incidents require
Revocation that happens in seconds rather than at someone's convenience
mentor.rule: Ticket creation records that something needs doing. Escalation handles nobody doing it. They are adjacent and separately named, and the exam tests the difference.
mentor.tell: An alert that generated no follow-up points to ticket creation. An alert that sat unactioned for a weekend points to escalation.
mentor.trap: Automating ticket creation on a noisy alert source multiplies the noise into a backlog. Tuning has to come first, or automation industrialises the problem.

label: What automation buys, and what it costs

mentor.diagnosis: You treated automation as free upside. The exam tests the trade: the same property that makes it valuable is what makes it dangerous.
contrast: Benefit
The same property, as a cost
Reaction time: it acts in seconds
It acts wrongly in seconds too, at full scale
Enforcing baselines: every host identical
One bad baseline is now on every host
Workforce multiplier: fewer hands needed
Those hands also held the knowledge of how it works
Standard configurations
Complexity and technical debt in the automation itself
One system does the provisioning
That system is a single point of failure
mentor.rule: Automation multiplies whatever you give it, including mistakes. Benefits scale and so does blast radius.
mentor.tell: 'Which is a drawback of automation' expects complexity, technical debt, single point of failure, or ongoing supportability, never 'it is slower'.
mentor.trap: Every listed benefit is genuinely true, so a benefits answer always reads as correct. Check whether the stem asked for the cost.

label: Guard rails vs ticket creation vs provisioning

mentor.diagnosis: You named an automation use case that does not match what the scenario automates. Each one automates a different moment.
contrast: Use case
What it automates
Scenario wording
User provisioning
Creating and removing accounts from an HR trigger
'A leaver still had access three weeks later'
Resource provisioning
Standing up infrastructure to a template
'Each environment was built slightly differently'
Guard rails
Blocking a non-compliant action as it is attempted
'Engineers could create a public storage bucket'
Security groups
Membership, and therefore access, from a rule
'Access is granted by job role automatically'
Ticket creation and escalation
Raising and routing the work item
'Alerts were seen but nobody was assigned'
Continuous integration and testing
Running checks on every change
'A bad config reached production unreviewed'
mentor.rule: Match the automation to the moment that failed. Access that lingered is provisioning; an action that should have been impossible is a guard rail; work nobody picked up is ticketing.
mentor.tell: Onboarding and offboarding stories are almost always user provisioning, and the exam likes the offboarding half because the risk is clearer.
mentor.trap: Guard rails and security groups both sound like preventing access. Guard rails stop an action; security groups decide membership.
